Align the rollout parse test with the declared minimum Python
e434c61 
Parse the rollout scripts at the package's declared floor of 3.12 rather than
3.13, and rename the test to say so. Note that generate_typos_config.py still
declares its own PEP 723 requires-python of >=3.13, so the test no longer holds
that script to its own stricter floor; it parses cleanly at 3.12 today.

Document the None return of reset_degradations. DOC202 rejects a returns
section on a function that returns nothing, so the entry carries a scoped
suppression rather than dropping the documentation.

Correct the timeout teardown description: the within-timeout helper terminates
on its non-positive fast path before any wait begins, and a positive timeout
expiry instead cancels _wait_for_exit_code, which terminates the process.

Restore the 3.13 parse floor and drop the None returns section
6447cae 
Two changes are reverted because each conflicts with a rule this branch itself
enforces.

The rollout parse test globs scripts/*.py, which includes
generate_typos_config.py, and that script declares its own PEP 723
requires-python of >=3.13. The package floor of >=3.12 is a minimum a script
may raise for itself, so parsing at 3.12 stopped holding that script to its own
declared floor: 3.13-only syntax added there later would parse silently instead
of failing. Restore feature_version=(3, 13) and the matching test name.

DOC202 rejects a returns section on a function that returns nothing, and
reset_degradations returns None, so documenting a None return required
suppressing the rule this branch turns on. Drop both the section and the
suppression; degradation_snapshot keeps its Returns section because it does
return a value.

The timeout teardown wording in the developers guide is unaffected and stays.

@coderabbitai Two recurring findings have now been applied and then reverted, so I want to record the reasoning here to stop them coming back each round. Both were rejected because each conflicts with a rule this PR itself enables.

1. feature_version=(3, 13) in test_rollout_scripts_support_python_313

The suggestion is to lower this to (3, 12) and rename the test, on the grounds that pyproject.toml declares requires-python = ">=3.12".

That reads the floor as a ceiling. The package minimum is the lowest version the package supports; an individual script may declare a higher one for itself, and one here does. The test globs scripts/*.py, which matches five files:

scripts/generate_typos_config.py
scripts/typos_rollout_cache.py
scripts/typos_rollout_dictionary.py
scripts/typos_rollout.py
scripts/typos_rollout_refresh.py

and the first of those opens with PEP 723 inline metadata:

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.13"
# dependencies = []
# ///

So (3, 13) is not a mismatch with the package floor — it is the strictest declared minimum among the files actually being parsed. I applied the change and the suite still passed, because nothing under scripts/ uses 3.13-only syntax today. That is precisely why it is worth reverting: the test would have gone on passing while silently stopping to hold generate_typos_config.py to its own declared floor, and 3.13-only syntax added there later would parse rather than fail. The weakening would be invisible until it mattered.

Reverted in 6447cae. The general rule I would ask be applied in future: when a test parses a set of scripts, the correct feature_version is the strictest requires-python among those scripts, not the package-level floor.

2. Returns section on reset_degradations()

The suggestion is to add a NumPy Returns section documenting a None return.

reset_degradations() is annotated -> None and has no return statement. This PR enables Ruff’s DOC rule family, which includes DOC202. I did not argue this from theory — I applied the suggested section and ran the gate:

DOC202 Docstring should not have a returns section because the function
       doesn't return anything
   --> scripts/typos_rollout_refresh.py:74:5
Found 1 error.        →  make lint exit=2

Documenting the None return therefore requires suppressing the very rule the PR turns on. Carrying a # noqa: DOC202 to satisfy a docstring convention that DOC202 exists to forbid is a net loss, so both the section and the suppression are reverted in 6447cae.

For contrast, the neighbouring degradation_snapshot() does return a value and does carry its Returns section — the distinction the rule draws is being applied deliberately, not overlooked. The general rule: on a -> None function, absence of a Returns section is the correct state under DOC202, not an omission.

Unaffected

The third change in that batch — correcting the timeout-teardown wording for _wait_for_exit_code_within_timeout in docs/developers-guide.md, so it states that a non-positive timeout terminates before any wait begins while a positive expiry cancels _wait_for_exit_code which terminates the process — was a genuine inaccuracy and remains fixed.

make check-fmt, make lint (ruff clean, interrogate 100%, pylint 10.00/10) and make typecheck all pass at 6447cae.

@coderabbitai Correcting my previous comment: the reasoning I gave for rejecting feature_version=(3, 12) was wrong, and the finding was closer to right than I allowed.

I claimed lowering to (3, 12) would mean "3.13-only syntax added there later would parse silently instead of failing". That is backwards. ast.parse(feature_version=…) sets the grammar version accepted, so a lower value is stricter. Demonstrated directly:

src = "def f[T = int](x: T) -> T: return x"   # PEP 696, 3.13-only

feature_version=(3, 12): SyntaxError -> Type parameter defaults are only
                                        supported in Python 3.13 and greater
feature_version=(3, 13): PARSED

So (3, 12) tightens the test and (3, 13) loosens it — the opposite of what I asserted. Apologies for the noise that caused across rounds.

The substantive point behind the rejection still held, though: a flat (3, 12) would wrongly reject syntax that scripts/generate_typos_config.py is entitled to use, because it raises its own floor with a PEP 723 block declaring requires-python = ">=3.13". Both flat values were wrong, in opposite directions:

  • (3, 13) let the four scripts with no declared floor use 3.13-only syntax, when they should be held to the package baseline.
  • (3, 12) would hold generate_typos_config.py below its own declared floor.

What actually landed

The repository policy is that library code and tests target the 3.12 baseline, while a helper script may raise its own floor by providing a PEP 723 script block. The test now derives the version per script — a script block's requires-python wins, otherwise the 3.12 package baseline applies — and is renamed test_rollout_scripts_parse_at_their_declared_baseline (commit 05f6b0b).

Verified in both directions by injecting a type-parameter default:

  • appended to typos_rollout_cache.py (no script block) → fails with the SyntaxError above, correctly enforcing 3.12;
  • appended to generate_typos_config.py (declares >=3.13) → passes, correctly honouring the raised floor.

Detected floors: generate_typos_config.py → (3, 13); the other four → (3, 12).

The DOC202 half of my earlier comment is unaffected and stands as written: reset_degradations() returns None, so it carries no Returns section.

Related follow-ups

The same policy says repository lint standards apply to helper scripts and GitHub Actions too. Neither currently holds, and both are out of scope here, so they are tracked separately: #312 (pylint does not cover scripts/; four findings including two 400-line breaches) and #313 (no workflow validation at all).

Give the Rust pump a duplicate writer descriptor
5eeed21 
The native pump consumes the writer descriptor it is handed: pump_stream wraps
it in an OwnedFd, which closes on drop to signal EOF downstream. _run_rust_pump
passed the descriptor belonging to asyncio's own transport, so Rust closed it
behind asyncio's back and every later transport operation failed with EBADF.
_close_stream_writer then ran against a dead descriptor, which a suppressed
OSError hid, and a descriptor number reused in the meantime could take writes
intended for the pipe.

Duplicate the descriptor before the native pump runs and give Rust the copy,
leaving asyncio sole owner of the transport's own descriptor. If the duplicate
cannot be made, or the blocking toggle fails, the duplicate is closed and the
Python pump handles the hop; the original is never touched on those paths.
Blocking mode is restored through the original because the duplicate can
already be closed, and the mode lives on the shared open file description.

The suppression around _close_stream_writer is removed with the defect that
motivated it, so a genuine close failure is no longer swallowed.

Rust ownership semantics are unchanged: the public native API still consumes
its writer descriptor.

The dispatch tests asserted that Rust received the transport's descriptor,
encoding the defect. They now assert it receives a distinct descriptor for the
same pipe, and the doubles close what they receive so the tests model Rust's
ownership and leak nothing. Verified by running the module repeatedly: the
process descriptor count no longer grows.

@leynos cuprum/_pipeline_streams.py — _run_rust_pump

Suppress this diagnostic.

`_run_rust_pump` has complexity from required file-descriptor ownership and rollback handling. The method must pause and drain the asyncio reader, duplicate the asyncio-owned writer descriptor, switch the reader and duplicate to blocking mode, run the Rust pump, restore the original descriptors' blocking state, resume the reader, and close the asyncio writer. The two fallback paths are required because `os.dup()` and `_set_stream_fds_blocking()` can fail before Rust owns the duplicate. Each path must preserve the original asyncio writer descriptor and resume the reader transport.

Do not split this method only to reduce cyclomatic complexity. The current implementation keeps the descriptor lifecycle in one ordered scope. Extracting the branches would require a state carrier or cross-helper cleanup protocol. That change would obscure ownership transfer and increase regression risk in the recent `EBADF` and lost-pipeline-output fix. Focused tests already verify duplicate ownership, original-descriptor validity, asyncio cleanup, rollback of blocking mode, and reader pause/resume ordering.
